fact: Many decisions arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound.
source_span: Many decisions are thought to arise via the accumulation of noisy evidence to a threshold or bound .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the fundamental decision-making mechanism studied in the article.

fact: In perception, the accumulation of noisy evidence explains how stimulus strength affects decision speed, accuracy, and confidence.
source_span: In perception , the mechanism explains the effect of stimulus strength , characterized by signal-to-noise ratio , on decision speed , accuracy and confidence .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides context for why the study focuses on noise and its effects on decision variables.

fact: An increase in noise is predicted to lead to faster decisions, reduced accuracy, and paradoxically higher confidence.
source_span: An increase in noise should lead to faster decisions , reduced accuracy and , paradoxically , higher confidence .
selection_reasoning: This is a key theoretical prediction that the study aims to test experimentally.

fact: The study introduced a novel sensory manipulation that mimics adding unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex.
source_span: To test these predictions , we introduce a novel sensory manipulation that mimics the addition of unbiased noise to motion-selective regions of visual cortex , which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the main experimental approach used to test the theoretical predictions.

fact: Neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST verified the sensory manipulation increased noise in motion-selective visual cortex.
source_span: which we verified with neuronal recordings from macaque areas MT/MST .
selection_reasoning: Verification of the manipulation in a relevant brain area supports the validity of the experimental method.

fact: Increasing noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence in both humans and monkeys over a range of stimuli with minimal impairment to accuracy.
source_span: For both humans and monkeys , increasing the noise induced faster decisions and greater confidence over a range of stimuli for which accuracy was minimally impaired .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding confirming key model predictions across species.

fact: The magnitude of the effects of noise on decision speed and confidence matched predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model.
source_span: The magnitude of the effects was in agreement with predictions of a bounded evidence accumulation model .
selection_reasoning: This fact links experimental results to the theoretical framework, supporting the model's validity.

fact: Decisions that combine information from different sources or over time serve as a model of cognitive function because they are not hardwired or reflexive but experimentally tractable.
source_span: Decisions that combine information from different sources or across time are of special interest to neuroscience because they serve as a model of cognitive function . These decisions are not hard wired or reflexive , yet they are experimentally tractable .
selection_reasoning: This background explains the significance of studying such decisions in neuroscience.

fact: Decision confidence is a graded belief in the accuracy of a choice that influences learning, planning, and communication.
source_span: Third , decisions are often accompanied by a graded degree of belief in the accuracy or appropriateness of the choice . This belief , referred to as decision confidence , influences many aspects of behavior: how we learn from our mistakes , plan subsequent decisions , and communicate our decisions to others .
selection_reasoning: This fact defines decision confidence and its behavioral relevance, important for understanding the study's focus.

fact: Bounded evidence accumulation models explain choice, reaction time, and confidence by integrating momentary evidence until a decision variable reaches a threshold.
source_span: The family of bounded evidence accumulation models , including drift diffusion , race and attractor models , offers one such framework for linking choice , reaction time and confidence ... The decision terminates when the accumulated evidence for one alternative , termed a decision variable ( DV ) , reaches a threshold or bound , thereby determining both the choice and the decision time . Confidence in the decision derives from a mapping between the DV and the probability that a decision based on this DV will be correct .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the theoretical model central to the study.

fact: Noise in momentary evidence causes the decision variable to fluctuate, influencing reaction time and confidence especially when signal-to-noise ratio is low.
source_span: The noisiness of the momentary evidence causes the DV to wander from its starting point , as in Brownian motion or diffusion , whereas the expectation ( i . e . , mean ) of the momentary evidence increments or decrements the DV deterministically . Noise is the main determinant of both RT and confidence when signal-to-noise is low , that is when choices are more stochastic ( less accurate ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the role of noise in decision dynamics, motivating the experimental manipulation.

fact: If noise is selectively increased without changing the mean evidence, bounded accumulation predicts lower accuracy with strong evidence, faster reaction times with weak evidence, and increased confidence with weak evidence.
source_span: Specifically , were it possible to leave unchanged the expectation of each sample of momentary evidence while boosting the noise associated with it , then the bounded accumulation of the noisier samples should lead to ( i ) lower accuracy when the expectation of the momentary evidence is strong , ( ii ) faster reaction times when the momentary evidence is weak , and ( iii ) increased confidence when the momentary evidence is weak .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the specific testable predictions that the study addresses.

fact: The study introduced a method to selectively increase the variance (volatility) of motion evidence in a random dot motion display without changing its mean motion strength.
source_span: We therefore sought a method to manipulate the variance associated with the neural representation of momentary evidence without affecting its mean. We achieved this with a manipulation of the motion information in a random dot motion (RDM) display, by adding a second level of randomness which increased its volatility but was unbiased with respect to the strength and direction of motion evidence.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key methodological innovation enabling the study to test the effect of noise on decision-making, which is central to the article's main question.

fact: Neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex represent momentary motion evidence and were used to verify the volatility manipulation.
source_span: We verified that the manipulation has the desired properties by recording from direction selective neurons in the middle temporal (MT) and medial superior temporal (MST) areas of the macaque visual cortex. Neurons in these areas are known to represent the momentary evidence in tasks identical to those in our study.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides biological validation of the stimulus manipulation, linking neural activity to the behavioral paradigm, which is important background and method-level information.

fact: The volatility manipulation increased the variance of motion energy and neural responses without changing the mean motion strength or mean neural response significantly.
source_span: For all motion strengths, the mean (upper) is not affected by the volatility manipulation, whereas the variance is larger in the high volatility condition. ... The volatility manipulation produced a small increase in the average firing rate at the low coherences (upper)... The variance parallels the mean, but volatility has a more marked effect on variance at weak motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes that the manipulation selectively increased noise (variance) rather than signal strength, which is critical for interpreting the study's findings on noise effects.

fact: The study tested the influence of increased noise (volatility) on choice accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in both monkeys and humans.
source_span: We then used the volatility manipulation to test the influence of noise on the three observables of choice behavior—accuracy, RT and confidence—in monkeys and humans.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main experimental question and the behavioral measures used, which are central to the article's principal findings.

fact: Previous methods to increase neural noise, such as transcranial magnetic stimulation or microstimulation, inferred effects from behavior but did not directly characterize neural signals underlying decision formation.
source_span: A dissociation between accuracy and confidence led Rahnev et al. (2012) to conclude that transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) increased the neural noise associated with the representation of a visual pattern... However, characterization of these effects of TMS and microstimulation was inferred from behavior. Similarly, psychophysical studies that attempted to increase the noise through changes in the visual stimulus or attentional state did not characterize the influence of these manipulations on the neural signals that the brain accumulates to form a decision.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides motivation for the study by highlighting limitations of prior approaches, justifying the need for the new volatility manipulation.

fact: The variance of motion energy is larger for high volatility stimuli compared to low volatility stimuli, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: A more systematic analysis of the motion energy , displayed in Figure 2B , reveals that the mean is identical for low and high volatility stimuli , for all motion strengths ( upper panel ) , whereas the variance is larger for the high volatility stimuli ( lower panel ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key difference in stimulus properties that affects neural processing and decision-making, central to the study's investigation of volatility effects.

fact: Direction selective neurons in cortical areas MT/MST represent momentary evidence used by monkeys to guide choice, reaction time, and confidence in motion discrimination tasks.
source_span: These neurons represent the momentary evidence used by monkeys to guide their choice , reaction time and confidence ( Salzman et al . , 1990; Celebrini and Newsome , 1995; Ditterich et al . , 2003; Fetsch et al . , 2014 ) in motion discrimination tasks .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological system and relevance of the neural signals studied.

fact: The firing rate of MT neurons increases linearly with motion strength in the preferred direction and decreases less steeply in the anti-preferred direction, producing a bilinear response function.
source_span: As previously shown ( Britten et al . , 1993 ) , the firing rate of MT neurons increases linearly , on average , as a function of motion strength in the neuron? preferred direction ( c?>?0 , Figure 2C , upper panel , blue trace ) . The firing rate decreases linearly , but less steeply , as a function of motion strength in the anti-preferred direction ( c?<?0 ) , giving rise to a bilinear function .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key neural response property relevant to understanding how motion strength affects neural signals.

fact: High volatility stimuli cause a subtle increase in firing rate at low motion coherences due to rectification of neural responses when the distribution of motion strength spans positive and negative values.
source_span: These features are preserved under high volatility ( red trace ) , but there is a subtle increase in firing rate at the low coherences , which is explained by the rectification of neural responses when the distribution of c spans positive and negative values ( Figure 2C , inset ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding links stimulus volatility to changes in neural firing patterns, a principal result.

fact: The variance of neural responses scales approximately linearly with firing rate, and high volatility adds to this variance especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: The variance of the neural response is known to scale approximately linearly with firing rate ( Tolhurst et al . , 1983; Vogels et al . , 1989; Geisler and Albrecht , 1997; Shadlen and Newsome , 1998 ) . Thus the variance curves in Figure 2C ( lower panel ) parallel the means . The high volatility condition adds to the variance in a manner that is exaggerated at the low motion strengths , consistent with the motion energy analysis above .
selection_reasoning: This fact connects stimulus volatility to neural variability, important for understanding decision-related neural signals.

fact: Momentary evidence for decision-making is assumed to be the difference between average firing rates from two pools of neurons with opposite direction preferences.
source_span: We assume that the momentary evidence is the difference between the average firing rates from two pools of neurons with direction preferences for the two opposite directions ( e . g . , right-preferring minus left-preferring ) ( Shadlen et al . , 1996; Ditterich et al . , 2003; Hanks et al . , 2006 ) .
selection_reasoning: This defines the key neural signal integrated during decision-making, central to the study's analysis.

fact: The mean of the difference in neural signals between opposing pools is similar for both low and high volatility conditions, but the variance of this difference is greater under high volatility.
source_span: The mean of the difference variable ( 弮? ) is similar for both volatility conditions ( upper ) , whereas the variance of the difference variable ( ??2 ) is greater under high volatility ( lower ) .
selection_reasoning: This principal finding links stimulus volatility to increased neural variability in decision-related signals.

fact: The correlation between opposing pools of neurons is negative because they respond oppositely to fluctuations in the motion stimulus.
source_span: The correlation is negative because the opposing pools respond oppositely to fluctuations in the motion stimulus .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic fact explains the relationship between neural pools relevant to interpreting the difference signal.

fact: The visual system blurs rapidly displayed random dot motion stimuli over time, creating the illusion that more dots are present simultaneously than are actually displayed.
source_span: The visual system blurs these images over time , leading for example to the illusion that many more dots are present simultaneously than are actually displayed .
selection_reasoning: This background fact helps explain the nature of the stimulus and its perceptual processing.

fact: An established motion filter applied to the stimuli extracts a time-blurred motion signal that approximates firing rates of direction selective neurons in primate visual cortex.
source_span: The right panel of Figure 2A applies an established motion filter ( Adelson and Bergen , 1985 ) to the example movies parameterized by the low and high volatility traces shown in the left panel ( see also Video 1 ) . The filter extracts a time-blurred motion signal that provides a reasonable approximation to the firing rates of direction selective neurons in the primate visual cortex ( Britten et al . , 1993; Rust et al . , 2006; Hedges et al . , 2011 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method linking stimulus properties to neural responses.

fact: The study investigated how changes in the variance of momentary sensory evidence affect decision speed, accuracy, and confidence in a bounded evidence accumulation framework.
source_span: In what follows we attempt to ascertain whether a change in the variance of the momentary evidence , introduced by our volatility manipulation , affects decision speed , accuracy , and confidence in accordance with the predictions of bounded evidence accumulation .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main research question and motivation, which is central to the abstract-level summary.

fact: The volatility manipulation increased the variance of momentary evidence, especially at weak motion strengths, without substantially affecting the mean evidence.
source_span: From these complementary analyses of stimulus and neural response , we conclude that the volatility manipulation has negligible effects on the expectation of momentary evidence and more substantial effects on the variance , especially at weak motion strengths .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key experimental manipulation and its effect on the sensory evidence, which is critical background for understanding the study.

fact: One monkey and three human subjects performed a direction discrimination task by indicating their choice with eye movements to one of two targets.
source_span: One monkey ( monkey W ) and three humans were required to decide between two possible directions of motion and , when ready , to indicate their decision by looking to one of two targets ( Figure 3A ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main experimental paradigm and participants, important for understanding the methods at a high level.

fact: Stronger motion coherence led to faster and more accurate choices in both high and low volatility conditions.
source_span: For both high and low volatility conditions , stronger motion led to faster and more accurate choices .
selection_reasoning: This fact states a principal behavioral finding that supports the validity of the task and data.

fact: High volatility decreased reaction times, especially at the weakest motion strengths, across all subjects.
source_span: The main effect of high volatility was to decrease RTs , particularly at the weakest motion strengths ( Figure 3B , bottom row , red ) . This effect was robust for all three human subjects and the monkey ( Equation 16 , all p<0 . 03 , t-test , H0: 帣2=0 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key experimental result linking volatility manipulation to decision speed, a core finding.

fact: The volatility manipulation had only subtle and statistically unreliable effects on accuracy for individual subjects in the reaction time task.
source_span: The manipulation affected the accuracy only subtly , and this was not statistically reliable for individual subjects in the RT task ( Figure 3B , top row; for the four subjects: p=[0 . 35 , 0 . 65 , 0 . 2 , 0 . 26] , Equation 17 , likelihood-ratio test ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact qualifies the effect of volatility on accuracy, important for interpreting the behavioral results.

fact: Pooling data across subjects and including confidence tasks revealed a significant effect of volatility on accuracy.
source_span: However , there was a significant effect of volatility on accuracy when pooling data across subjects and including data from the confidence tasks described below ( Equation 18 , p<0 . 0005 , likelihood ratio test , H0: 帣2=0; see also Figure 3?igure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact indicates a more subtle but statistically significant effect of volatility on accuracy when considering more data, relevant for the overall conclusions.

fact: Subjects reported their decision about motion direction by making a saccadic eye movement to the corresponding target.
source_span: Subjects reported their decision by making a saccadic eye movement to the right ( left ) target for rightward ( leftward ) motion.
selection_reasoning: This describes the behavioral response method used to measure decision-making, a key aspect of the experimental design.

fact: Trials with different motion coherences and volatilities were randomly interleaved during the experiment.
source_span: Trials of different coherences and volatilities were randomly interleaved.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the experimental manipulation and design relevant to testing the effect of volatility on decision-making.

fact: High volatility had only weak effects on accuracy but shortened reaction times for all subjects, especially at low motion strengths.
source_span: High volatility had only weak effects on accuracy ( upper ) but shortened the reaction times for all subjects ( lower ) , particularly at the low motion strengths.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about how stimulus volatility affects decision speed and accuracy.

fact: The pattern of results is consistent with decisions being made when an accumulation of noisy evidence reaches a bound, as modeled by a bounded evidence accumulation (drift diffusion) model.
source_span: The pattern of results in Figure 3B is consistent with the hypothesis that decisions are made when an accumulation of noisy evidence reaches a bound.
selection_reasoning: This provides a key mechanistic interpretation of the behavioral data, central to the study's scientific claims.

fact: Increased stimulus volatility increases the variance of momentary evidence, which accelerates the time to reach a decision bound and thus shortens reaction times.
source_span: The effect of increased volatility on RT is most apparent at motion strengths near zero ... by increasing noise , the volatility manipulation accelerates the dispersion of the decision variable away from its expected value and nearer the termination bounds , hence faster RT.
selection_reasoning: This explains the mechanism by which volatility affects decision speed, a core scientific insight.

fact: Volatility mainly affects reaction times at weak motion strengths where accuracy is already poor, explaining why volatility has subtle effects on accuracy but strong effects on reaction time.
source_span: The volatility manipulation mainly affects the weakest motion strengths where accuracy is already poor ... This helps to reconcile the contrast between the striking effects of volatility on RT versus subtle effects on choice accuracy.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the differential impact of volatility on accuracy versus reaction time, a key interpretive point.

fact: Confidence in a decision can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time in a bounded evidence accumulation framework.
source_span: Confidence refers to the belief that a decision one is about to make ( or has just made ) is likely to be correct . In the framework of bounded evidence accumulation , it can be formalized as the conditional probability of a correct choice given the state of the DV , which comprises the accumulated evidence and elapsed decision time.
selection_reasoning: This defines confidence in a way that links it mechanistically to the decision process, important for understanding subsequent findings.

fact: Increased volatility mimics an increase in the diffusion rate, accelerating the decision variable away from neutral and thus increasing confidence at low motion coherences.
source_span: Increased volatility should affect confidence because it mimics an increase in the diffusion rate ... its main effect on the DV is to accelerate its exodus away from neutral ... Therefore , we predicted that volatility would increase confidence at low coherences.
selection_reasoning: This is a key hypothesis and mechanistic prediction about how volatility affects confidence, central to the study.

fact: A monkey was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering, allowing it to opt out of the direction choice for a smaller but certain reward.
source_span: Monkey D was trained on a motion discrimination task with post-decision wagering ... On half of the trials , the monkey had the opportunity to opt out of reporting the direction choice and to select instead a smaller but certain reward.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key experimental method used to measure confidence behaviorally in a non-human primate.

fact: The 'sure bet' option was presented only after motion offset during a memory delay, encouraging the monkey to perform the direction discrimination on every trial.
source_span: The 'sure bet' option was not revealed until at least one-half second after motion offset ( i . e . , during the delay ) . The task design thus encouraged the monkey to perform the direction discrimination on every trial.
selection_reasoning: This detail explains the task design that ensures the monkey engages with the decision before opting out, relevant to interpreting confidence measures.

fact: After extensive experience with the low volatility random dot motion task, high volatility stimuli were introduced on a random half of the trials.
source_span: After extensive experience with the standard RDM ( >100 , 000 trials; low volatility condition ) , we introduced the high volatility RDM on a random half of the trials.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the experimental manipulation critical to testing the effect of volatility on decision-making and confidence.

fact: The study investigated how stimulus volatility affects decision confidence in both monkeys and humans performing motion direction discrimination tasks.
source_span: The main question we wished to address is whether the high volatility condition would elicit fewer sure-bet choices, consistent with greater confidence.
selection_reasoning: This fact states the core research question motivating the study, which is essential for an abstract-aligned summary.

fact: Monkeys performed a motion direction discrimination task where they could opt for a sure-bet option that gave a small but certain reward during a delay period.
source_span: The monkey viewed the motion display for random duration, controlled by the computer, followed by a memory-delay period. When the fixation point was extinguished, the monkey indicated the net direction of motion by making an eye movement to a left or right choice target in order to receive a liquid reward, if correct. On a random half of trials, the monkey was presented a third “sure bet” option (red target) during the delay period, which if chosen resulted in a small but certain reward.
selection_reasoning: This describes the key behavioral task and the sure-bet option, which is central to measuring confidence in the monkey.

fact: High stimulus volatility caused monkeys to waive the sure-bet option more often, indicating increased decision confidence despite no systematic change in accuracy.
source_span: The proportion of trials the monkey decided to waive the sure-bet option (deciding instead for a riskier direction choice) was greater on the high volatility trials... Thus, high volatility increased the monkey’s confidence, and did so despite a negligible effect on accuracy.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking volatility to confidence, a core scientific claim.

fact: Monkeys were more likely to opt out of making a direction decision by choosing the sure bet when the evidence was weak or the stimulus duration was brief, improving accuracy on trials where they made a direction choice.
source_span: In both low and high volatility conditions, the monkey made rational use of the sure bet, opting out more often for weaker motion... and for briefer stimuli... When the sure bet was offered but waived, choice accuracy was higher than when the sure bet was not offered.
selection_reasoning: This finding supports the interpretation that the sure-bet choice reflects trial-by-trial confidence, important for understanding the behavioral mechanism.

fact: Human participants performing a similar motion discrimination task with fixed stimulus duration also reported higher confidence ratings for high volatility stimuli, especially at low motion coherence.
source_span: We confirmed the relationship between volatility and confidence in human participants... They also reported higher confidence for the high volatility stimuli, and the effect was most apparent for the low coherence stimuli.
selection_reasoning: This extends the main finding to humans, supporting the generality and translational relevance of the results.

fact: Volatility did not systematically affect accuracy in either monkeys or humans during the motion discrimination tasks.
source_span: Volatility did not affect accuracy systematically... Naturally, subjects were more confident for high coherence stimuli... Volatility again did not affect accuracy systematically.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies that confidence changes were not due to changes in objective performance, a key interpretive point.

fact: The study investigates how motion strength and volatility affect choice, accuracy, reaction time, and confidence in perceptual decision-making.
source_span: So far , the effect of volatility has been described qualitatively . Now we show how a single bounded accumulation model can account for the combined effect of motion strength and volatility on choice , accuracy and RT .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main research question and the variables studied, which is central to the abstract-level summary.

fact: A bounded accumulation model explains choice, reaction time, and confidence by accumulating noisy momentary evidence until a decision threshold is reached or the stimulus ends.
source_span: In the model , choice , RT and confidence result from the accumulation of noisy momentary evidence as a function of time , until the integral of the evidence ( the decision variable , DV ) reaches one of two bounds , or for the PDW and confidence tasks , until the stimulus is curtailed .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key modeling approach used to explain the behavioral data, important for understanding the study's method and findings.

fact: The variance of momentary evidence increases with motion strength, and the difference in noise between volatility conditions is largest at zero coherence and decreases with stronger motion.
source_span: These analyses showed that ( i ) the variance of the momentary evidence increases with motion strength , and ( ii ) the difference in noise between volatility conditions is larger at 0% coherence and decays gradually for stronger motion .
selection_reasoning: This finding about noise characteristics is central to how the model accounts for the effects of volatility and motion strength.

fact: The model assumes that the brain has implicit knowledge of the accumulated evidence state, elapsed decision time, and how these map to the probability of making a correct choice to explain confidence judgments.
source_span: The framework can explain confidence if we assume that the brain has implicit knowledge of ( i ) the state of the accumulated evidence , ( ii ) the elapsed deliberation time , and ( iii ) the mapping of time and evidence to the probability of making a correct choice ( Figure 1C ) .
selection_reasoning: This assumption is key to linking the model to confidence, a principal outcome of the study.

fact: The model fits to human data show that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in perceptual choices, even when noise is experimentally controlled.
source_span: These predictions capture the trend well , supporting the notion that time and accumulated evidence are the main determinants of confidence in a perceptual choice , even when noise is under experimental control .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding validating the model's explanatory power for confidence judgments.

fact: The influence of motion strength and volatility on choice, reaction time, and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation across tasks and species.
source_span: The overall quality of the fits?cross all tasks and both species?ndicates that the influence of motion strength and volatility on choice , reaction time and confidence can be explained by a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the main conclusion and significance of the study.

fact: Many previous studies assumed that the variance of momentary evidence is fixed and independent of motion strength, but this study shows that variance increases with motion strength due to partial rectification in neural responses.
source_span: Many studies make the simplifying assumption that the variance of the momentary evidence is fixed and independent of motion strength ... However , the partial rectification ( Figure 2C ) implies that the variance of the difference should increase as a function of motion strength .
selection_reasoning: This background and motivation fact explains why the current study's approach is novel and necessary.

fact: Subjects do not revise the mapping between decision variable and confidence based on the noisiness (volatility) of incoming evidence during the task.
source_span: Thus, we assume that subjects do not infer the noisiness of incoming evidence, or that if they do, they do not revise the mapping accordingly.
selection_reasoning: This assumption is central to the study's modeling approach and interpretation of confidence judgments under different volatility conditions.

fact: The brain could, in principle, infer the noisiness of the stimulus in real time to adjust decision parameters or confidence evaluation.
source_span: An alternative is that the brain infers an estimate of the noisiness of the stimulus, in real time, to adjust the parameters of the decision process (Deneve, 2012; Qamar et al., 2013) or the evaluation of confidence (Yeung and Summerfield, 2012).
selection_reasoning: This background motivates testing models that incorporate volatility-dependent mappings and informs the study's main question about how volatility affects confidence.

fact: The sample mean and variance of motion energy can classify volatility conditions with 90% accuracy.
source_span: This is a reasonable proposition, at least in principle, because the sample mean and variance of the motion energy can be used to classify volatility conditions with 90% accuracy (see Materials and methods).
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the feasibility of the brain detecting volatility, which is relevant to the study's hypothesis and modeling.

fact: Models that use separate mappings between decision variable and confidence for high and low volatility conditions fit the behavioral data worse than a model using a common mapping.
source_span: When fit to data, this two-map model produces visibly worse fits than the model that relies on a common map, despite having the same number of parameters.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding that challenges the idea that subjects adjust confidence mappings based on volatility.

fact: A model assuming subjects have full and immediate knowledge of volatility on each trial reduces the effect of volatility on confidence but fits data worse than a common-map model.

fact: A model where subjects gradually learn volatility during a trial fits data similarly to the common-map model, with an estimated very slow rate of volatility information accrual.

fact: Allowing different decision bounds for high and low volatility trials does not improve model fits compared to a common-bound model in the post-decision wagering task.

fact: The analyses support the assumption that subjects applied a common mapping and decision strategy on trials of low and high volatility in this study.

selection_reasoning: This is a key conclusion about how subjects process volatility in the experimental context.

fact: It is unclear whether subjects performed suboptimally or were unable to identify volatility conditions without additional costs such as effort or time.

fact: Neurons in the MT/MST areas of the brain represent momentary evidence used to inform decisions and confidence.

fact: The study used simultaneous transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) and functional MRI (fMRI) to investigate neural mechanisms underlying externally induced oscillatory synchronization.

fact: Two experiments were conducted with healthy adult volunteers performing cognitive tasks under different tACS conditions.
source_span: Experiment 1 included 10 healthy volunteers ... In Experiment 2 , 24 healthy volunteers ... participated in the study .

fact: Participants performed cognitive tasks including a choice-reaction task (CRT) and N-back working memory tasks with varying difficulty levels.
source_span: Participants performed tasks with different levels of cognitive difficulty . In Experiment 1 participants performed two tasks , the choice-reaction task ( CRT ) and two versions of the N-back task: 1-back and 2-back .
selection_reasoning: Describes the behavioral tasks used to probe cognitive function, key to the study's measurements.

fact: The CRT task measures general alertness and motor speed by requiring participants to respond quickly and accurately to left or right pointing arrows.
source_span: The CRT is a 2-alternative force choice paradigm used for testing general alertness and motor speed . Participants were instructed to respond as quickly and as accurately as possible , with the right or left index finger , to the presentation of a right or left pointing arrow ...
selection_reasoning: Defines one of the main tasks and its cognitive relevance, necessary background for interpreting results.

fact: The N-back task assesses working memory by requiring participants to detect whether a current digit matches one presented one or two trials earlier.
source_span: The N-back is a WM task that requires on-line monitoring , and manipulation of remembered information . ... In the 2-back task participants detected a repetition of the digit occurring two trials before , whereas in the 1-back task they detected whether the stimulus matched the one presented in the previous trial .
selection_reasoning: Explains the key cognitive process tested by the N-back task, important for understanding the study's focus on working memory.

fact: tACS was applied at 6 Hz frequency with electrodes placed at scalp locations F4 and P4, with either synchronous (0° phase offset) or desynchronous (180° phase offset) stimulation conditions.
source_span: Stimulation was sinusoidal , 6 Hz frequency ... TACS was delivered in two different conditions: ( 1 ) Synchronous condition ( 0° ) ... ( 2 ) Desynchronous condition ( 180° ) ...
selection_reasoning: Describes the key experimental manipulation of brain stimulation, central to the study's hypothesis testing.

fact: In Experiment 1, participants completed sessions with synchronous tACS, desynchronous tACS, and sham stimulation in a pseudo-randomized cross-over design.
source_span: In Experiment 1 , participants performed one session of each tACS condition and sham in a pseudo-randomized cross-over design .
selection_reasoning: Summarizes the experimental design controlling for stimulation conditions, important for interpreting results.

fact: In Experiment 2, tACS was applied in short trains during task and fixation blocks to measure neural entrainment without increasing oscillatory power due to aftereffects.
source_span: In Experiment 2 , tACS was applied in a pseudo-randomized order for the duration of task ( 30s ) or fixation blocks ( 20s ) ... The application of short trains of tACS has the advantage of allowing the measurement of many periods of neural entrainment without an increase of oscillatory power due to tACS aftereffects ( Vossen et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: Highlights a methodological refinement to isolate neural entrainment effects, relevant to the study's approach.

fact: The study aimed to investigate how synchronous versus desynchronous tACS modulates brain activity and cognitive performance during working memory and reaction time tasks.
source_span: The sample size in Experiment 1 was chosen based on the effect sizes , between synchronous and desynchronous stimulation , observed in a previous study showing phase-dependent tACS modulations of RTs in a WM task ...
selection_reasoning: States the main scientific question and rationale behind comparing stimulation conditions.

fact: All participants were healthy adults with no history of neurological or psychiatric illness and provided informed consent under ethical approval.
source_span: All subjects were educated to degree level or above , with no history of neurological or psychiatric illness . Participants gave written informed consent . The study conforms to the Declaration of Helsinki and ethical approval was granted through the local ethics board ...
selection_reasoning: Provides important ethical and participant health context relevant to the study's validity.

fact: Short trains of transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) allow measurement of neural entrainment without increasing oscillatory power due to aftereffects.
source_span: The application of short trains of tACS has the advantage of allowing the measurement of many periods of neural entrainment without an increase of oscillatory power due to tACS aftereffects ( Vossen et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key methodological advantage of the stimulation protocol relevant to interpreting neural effects.

fact: Participants performed tasks under different tACS conditions including synchronous and desynchronous stimulation during 2-back and CRT tasks.

selection_reasoning: This describes the experimental design central to testing the effects of tACS on cognitive tasks.

fact: Experiment 2 was optimized to detect neurophysiological changes due to tACS by increasing signal-to-noise ratio and enabling psycho-physiological interaction analyses.
source_span: Experiment 2 was optimized to detect neurophysiological changes due to tACS by increasing signal-to-noise ratio and allowing computation of psycho-physiological interaction analyses .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the study's methodological focus on detecting brain connectivity changes induced by tACS.

fact: The tACS montage used did not cause artifacts in the fMRI signal, ensuring valid neuroimaging data during stimulation.
source_span: In agreement with previous studies ( Antal et al . , 2014; Cabral-Calderin et al . , 2016 ) the tACS montage employed in the study did not cause image artifacts .
selection_reasoning: This supports the validity of combining tACS with fMRI, a key methodological point.

fact: Electric field distributions on the cortex were modeled for synchronous and desynchronous tACS conditions using realistic finite element head models.
source_span: For each subject that took part in Experiment 2 we computed the electric field distributions on the cortex resulting from the two tACS conditions using a realistic finite element model as implemented in SimNibs 2 . 0 ( Opitz et al . , 2015; Thielscher et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method used to understand how tACS affects brain regions.

fact: Participants were blind to the stimulation condition and reported no significant differences in side effects between synchronous, desynchronous, and sham tACS conditions.
source_span: Participants were blind to the stimulation condition applied . At the end of each experiment , participants completed a questionnaire to assess possible side-effects of the tACS stimulation ... There was no significant difference between tACS conditions ( synchronous , desynchronous and sham ) for any of the side effects ( Chi Square tests ) , for Experiment 1 .
selection_reasoning: This supports the validity of the blinding and tolerability of the stimulation, important for interpreting behavioral and neural effects.

fact: Participants demonstrated low accuracy in detecting whether tACS stimulation was applied, indicating effective blinding between stimulation and non-stimulation periods.
source_span: In Experiment 2 , participants??demonstrated low accuracy for correctly detecting stimulation blocks ... which were explained by participants either perceiving stimulation during non-stimulation periods , or not perceiving the stimulation at all .
selection_reasoning: This fact confirms that participant awareness did not confound the experimental conditions.

fact: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors.
source_span: The granular retrosplenial cortex ( RSG ) is critical for both spatial and non-spatial behaviors , but the underlying neural codes remain poorly understood .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides essential background on the functional importance of the RSG, motivating the study.

fact: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) integrates inputs from multiple cortical and subcortical sources and is part of the brain's default mode network.
source_span: The RSG is also among the most densely connected regions of the brain , integrating inputs from a bevy of cortical and subcortical sources and serving as part of the default mode network ( Greicius et al . , 2009; Kaboodvand et al . , 2018; Liu et al . , 2019; Whitesell et al . , 2021 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the anatomical context and significance of the RSG in brain networks, relevant for understanding its function.

fact: The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum provide spatial information inputs that selectively recruit low-rheobase (LR) pyramidal cells in the superficial layers of the RSG.
source_span: The anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum , sources of spatial information , strongly and selectively recruit small low-rheobase ( LR ) pyramidal cells in RSG .
selection_reasoning: This is a key finding linking specific spatial inputs to a defined neuronal subtype in the RSG.

fact: Claustral and anterior cingulate cortex inputs, which carry mostly non-spatial information, preferentially control neighboring regular-spiking (RS) pyramidal cells in the superficial RSG.
source_span: In contrast , neighboring regular-spiking ( RS ) cells are preferentially controlled by claustral and anterior cingulate inputs , sources of mostly non-spatial information .
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies distinct input pathways targeting a different neuronal subtype, highlighting parallel processing.

fact: Precise sublaminar axonal and dendritic arborization within layer 1 of the RSG permits parallel processing of spatial and non-spatial inputs.
source_span: Precise sublaminar axonal and dendritic arborization within RSG layer 1 , in particular , permits this parallel processing .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic detail explains how anatomical organization supports functional segregation of inputs.

fact: Thalamocortical synaptic dynamics enable low-rheobase (LR) neurons in the RSG to compute the speed of head rotation despite receiving head direction inputs that do not explicitly encode speed.
source_span: Observed thalamocortical synaptic dynamics enable computational models of LR neurons to compute the speed of head rotation , despite receiving head direction inputs that do not explicitly encode speed .
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals a novel computational role for LR neurons in spatial orientation.

fact: Parallel input streams identify a distinct principal neuronal subtype in the RSG that is ideally positioned to support spatial orientation computations.
source_span: Thus , parallel input streams identify a distinct principal neuronal subtype ideally positioned to support spatial orientation computations in the RSG .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the significance of the parallel circuits and neuronal subtype specialization.

fact: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors including spatial navigation, learning, memory, fear conditioning, imagination, and planning for the future.
source_span: Activity in the granular retrosplenial cortex ( RSG ) is correlated with a wide variety of behaviors , including spatial navigation , learning , memory , fear conditioning , imagination , and planning for the future ( Alexander et al . , 2020; Alexander and Nitz , 2017; Chang et al . , 2020; Chrastil , 2018; Hinman et al . , 2018; Mao et al . , 2018; Miller et al . , 2021; Miller et al . , 2019 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact highlights the broad behavioral relevance of the RSG.

fact: The RSG receives inputs from thalamic nuclei, claustrum, anterior cingulate cortex, and other cortical areas, but the functional nature and cell-type specificity of these inputs have been insufficiently explored.
source_span: While these anatomical connections are well-documented ... few studies have examined their functional nature ... and cell-type specificity has yet to be sufficiently explored .
selection_reasoning: This fact motivates the study by identifying a knowledge gap about input specificity in the RSG.

fact: The anterior thalamus contains the highest proportion of head direction cells in the brain and projects matrix thalamocortical inputs predominantly to layer 1 of many cortical regions including the RSG.
source_span: Matrix thalamocortical ( TC ) inputs from the anterior thalamus , which contains the highest proportion of head direction cells in the brain ( Taube and Bassett , 2003 ) , influence layer 5 pyramidal cells in RSG ( Yamawaki et al . , 2019b ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background on the source and nature of spatial information inputs to the RSG.

fact: The claustrum projects to the RSG and innervates both excitatory and inhibitory neurons via precise laminar targeting, but the functional nature and subtype-specificity of claustral inputs to RSG neurons have not been investigated.
source_span: The cortex , including the RSG , also receives widespread inputs from the densely connected claustrum ... no studies have investigated the functional nature or subtype-specificity of ClaC inputs to RSG neurons .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a gap in knowledge about non-spatial input pathways to the RSG.

fact: Within the superficial layers of the RSG, two principal excitatory pyramidal neuron subtypes exist with distinct physiology and morphology: low-rheobase (LR) neurons and regular-spiking (RS) neurons.
source_span: Within the RSG , the superficial layers contain two subtypes of principal excitatory pyramidal neurons that have strikingly distinct physiology , morphology , and computational capabilities: the low-rheobase ( LR ) neuron and the regular-spiking ( RS ) neuron ( Brennan et al . , 2020; Kurotani et al . , 2013; Yousuf et al . , 2020 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact defines the key neuronal subtypes studied and their relevance to the circuit mechanisms.

fact: The granular retrosplenial cortex (RSG) contains two types of principal pyramidal neurons in its superficial layers: low-rheobase (LR) neurons and regular-spiking (RS) neurons.
source_span: Layer 3 of the granular retrosplenial cortex ( RSG ) contains two types of principal pyramidal neurons: the low-rheobase ( LR ) neuron and the regular-spiking ( RS ) neuron ( Brennan et al . , 2020; Kurotani et al . , 2013; Yousuf et al . , 2020 ).
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the key neuronal subtypes studied and is essential to understand the study's focus.

fact: Anterior thalamic and dorsal subicular inputs preferentially target LR neurons in the superficial RSG, while claustral and anterior cingulate inputs preferentially target RS neurons.
source_span: Specifically , we find that anterior thalamus and dorsal subiculum preferentially control LR neurons , whereas claustrum and anterior cingulate control RS cells .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding revealing a double dissociation in input targeting, central to the study's main claim about parallel processing.

fact: Channelrhodopsin-assisted circuit mapping (CRACM) was used to study subtype-specific circuits formed by anterior thalamic, claustral, anterior cingulate, and dorsal subicular inputs to the RSG.
source_span: Here , we use channelrhodopsin ( ChR2 ) -assisted circuit mapping ( CRACM ) to study the subtype-specific circuits formed by anterior thalamic , claustral , anterior cingulate , and dorsal subicular inputs to the RSG .
selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is important to understand how the study investigated input specificity.

fact: Anterior thalamic inputs to the RSG are localized predominantly in layer 1a and layer 3, where they overlap with the dendrites of LR neurons but not RS neurons.
source_span: Apical dendrites of LR neurons were most densely localized to L1a , with basal dendrites remaining confined to L3 ... RS apical dendrites rarely entered L1a ... Projection density analysis showed localization of ADAV axons and terminal arbors in L1a and weakly in L3 ... dendrites of LR , but not RS , cells selectively co-localize within layers 1a and 3 with ADAV TC afferents.
selection_reasoning: This anatomical finding explains the cellular basis for the preferential targeting of LR neurons by anterior thalamic inputs.

fact: LR neurons respond with significantly larger excitatory postsynaptic potentials and increased spiking to anterior thalamic input stimulation compared to RS neurons.
source_span: From resting membrane potentials ... LR neurons were strongly driven past spike threshold by these thalamic inputs while RS neurons exhibited far smaller EPSPs ... this stimulation evoked a significant increase in spiking in LR neurons ... but not RS neurons ... LR neurons thus had a significantly larger increase in spike rate evoked by the optical pulse than RS neurons.
selection_reasoning: This functional evidence supports the conclusion that LR neurons are the main recipients of anterior thalamic input.

fact: The synaptic dynamics of anterior thalamic inputs enable LR neurons to robustly encode angular speed, despite these inputs only explicitly containing head direction information.
source_span: We show that the synaptic dynamics of thalamic inputs allow for the robust encoding of angular speed by LR cell models , even though these inputs only explicitly contain information about head direction , not speed .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight links the input properties to the functional role of LR neurons in spatial orientation.

fact: LR neurons are ideally positioned to contribute to initial spatial orientation computations performed in superficial RSG.
source_span: Together , our results suggest that LR neurons are ideally positioned to contribute to the initial spatial orientation computations performed in superficial RSG .
selection_reasoning: This statement summarizes the significance and implication of the findings for spatial cognition.

fact: LR neurons in the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG) receive and process head direction inputs from the anterior thalamus more strongly than layer 3 or 5 regular spiking (RS) neurons.
source_span: This suggests that LR neurons , rather than layer 3 or 5 RS neurons , are the predominant RSG cell type receiving and processing head direction inputs from the anterior thalamus .
selection_reasoning: Identifies the main cell type in RSG responsible for processing head direction signals, a core finding about circuit function.

fact: LR neurons have the largest excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) amplitudes when anterior thalamic inputs target layer 1a, corresponding to the peak projection density of anterior dorsal anterior ventral (ADAV) axons.
source_span: We found that LR neurons have the largest EPSP amplitude when the LED pulse is targeting layer 1a , corresponding with the peak projection density of ADAV axons and terminal arbors at this lamina .
selection_reasoning: Shows the precise laminar targeting of thalamic inputs to LR neurons, explaining their strong response.

fact: RS neurons show much smaller EPSP amplitudes in response to anterior thalamic inputs and no significant variation in response across cortical layers.
source_span: In contrast , the RS neuron showed much smaller EPSP amplitude with no significant variation in response across the layers .
selection_reasoning: Highlights the difference in thalamic input responsiveness between LR and RS neurons, a key comparative finding.

fact: The laminar pattern of functional responses in LR neurons aligns precisely with the lamination of ADAV axons and terminal arbors in superficial layers of RSG.
source_span: This lamination of functional responses in the LR population precisely aligns with the lamination of ADAV axons and terminal arbors within these superficial layers .
selection_reasoning: Connects anatomical input patterns with functional responses, supporting the mechanism of LR neuron specialization.

fact: LR neurons lack dendrites in layer 5 and show no EPSP response to anterior thalamic stimulation in this layer.
source_span: L5dp responses were significantly smaller than those at L1/2 , as would be expected given the complete lack of LR dendrites in L5 .
selection_reasoning: Explains the anatomical basis for the absence of thalamic input response in deeper layers for LR neurons.

fact: The connectivity between anterior thalamic thalamocortical (TC) arbors and layer 3 principal neurons in RSG depends on precise sublaminar colocalization of dendrites and incoming thalamocortical axons.
source_span: Thus , the connectivity between anterior thalamic TC arbors and L3 principal neurons in RSG highlights a circuit that depends on the precise sublaminar colocalization of both local principal cells’ dendrites and incoming thalamocortical axons .
selection_reasoning: Summarizes the key circuit principle underlying selective input targeting.

fact: Approximately 60% of neurons in the anterior thalamus are head direction cells, providing directional information to LR neurons in RSG.
source_span: This demonstrates that LR neurons are uniquely anatomically adapted to respond to incoming inputs from the anterior thalamus , where ~60% of neurons are head direction cells .
selection_reasoning: Provides biological context for the importance of anterior thalamic inputs to LR neurons.

fact: Claustrum (CLA) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) provide major inputs to RSG that have distinct laminar projection patterns different from anterior thalamic inputs.
source_span: Two other main sources of input to RSG are the claustrum ( CLA ) and anterior cingulate cortex ( ACC ) . Both claustrocortical ( ClaC ) and ACC corticocortical ( CC ) projections have been anatomically shown to exhibit distinct laminar organization within its target cortical layers .
selection_reasoning: Introduces other important inputs to RSG and their distinct anatomical organization, relevant for understanding input specificity.

fact: RS neurons, but not LR neurons, receive strong claustral inputs in layers 1c, 2, and 5 of RSG.
source_span: Dendritic lamination plots of LR and RS dendrites and projection density plots of CLA axons and terminal arbors show that RS , but not LR , apical dendrites anatomically overlap with CLA arbors in superficial layers 1 c and two and upper layer 5 .
selection_reasoning: Identifies the cell type specificity of claustral inputs, contrasting with thalamic input targeting.

fact: RS neurons have significantly larger EPSP responses to claustral inputs compared to LR neurons, especially at layer 1/2 and layer 5.
source_span: We found that RS neurons have significantly larger responses to CLA input compared to LR neurons when stimulated at layer 1/2 . Similarly , layer 5 RS neurons exhibited significantly larger EPSP amplitudes in response to CLA inputs compared to LR cells .
selection_reasoning: Demonstrates functional specificity of claustral inputs to RS neurons, a key comparative finding.

fact: The laminar pattern of functional responses in RS neurons to claustral inputs aligns with the lamination of claustral axons and terminal arbors in layers 1c and 5.
source_span: This lamination of functional responses in the RS cell precisely aligns with the lamination of ClaC axons and terminal arbors within these layers .
selection_reasoning: Links anatomical input patterns with functional responses for claustral inputs, supporting the mechanism of RS neuron specialization.

fact: LR neurons show little to no EPSP response to claustral input stimulation at any laminar location in RSG.
source_span: In contrast , the complementary LR cell had no response to LED stimulation at any of the laminar locations .
selection_reasoning: Highlights the lack of claustral input to LR neurons, emphasizing input specificity.

fact: Regular spiking (RS) neurons in layer 3 of the retrosplenial granular cortex (RSG) receive stronger inputs from claustrum (ClaC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) afferents targeting the lower divisions of layer 1 (L1b/c and L1c).
source_span: Population analysis showed that within the RS cell population, RS cells have significantly larger responses at L1/2 and L5sup compared to those at L1a... corticocortical inputs from the anterior cingulate target L1b/c and, to a lesser extent, L5... overlapping precisely with RS, but not LR, dendrites.
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies the specific input sources and laminar targeting of RS neurons, a core finding about circuit specificity relevant to the study's main question.

fact: Low-rheobase (LR) neurons in layer 3 of RSG receive stronger thalamocortical inputs from the anterior dorsal thalamic nucleus (ADAV) and dorsal subiculum (DS) that target upper layer 1 (L1a) and layer 3, respectively.
source_span: Thalamocortical inputs preferentially target the apical dendrites of LR cells in upper L1 (L1a)... DS afferents to layer 3 of RSG precisely overlap with LR basal and, to a lesser degree, proximal apical dendrites... LR neurons responded with significantly larger EPSPs compared to RS neurons when DS inputs were stimulated at the cell body in layer 3.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the distinct input sources and laminar targeting of LR neurons, central to understanding parallel processing circuits in RSG.

fact: Claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex inputs preferentially target RS neurons, while anterior dorsal thalamic and dorsal subicular inputs preferentially target LR neurons in RSG.
source_span: Thus, inputs from both the dorsal subiculum and anterior thalamus target LR cells... while the claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex instead target RS cells.
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the main conclusion about parallel, cell-type-specific input pathways in RSG, a principal finding of the study.

fact: The precise sublaminar organization of afferent axons and layer 3 principal cell apical dendrites enables parallel processing of thalamocortical versus claustrocortical and corticocortical information in RSG.
source_span: This again indicates that parallel circuits in RSG process TC versus ClaC and CC information, and this parallel processing is enabled by precise sublaminar organization of afferent axons and layer three principal cell apical dendrites.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the significance of the anatomical and functional findings in terms of circuit organization and information processing.

fact: Dorsal subiculum inputs to RSG overlap with LR cell bodies and basal dendrites and evoke larger excitatory postsynaptic currents in superficial neurons compared to layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
source_span: Previous work has shown that dorsal subiculum... also precisely targets layer 2/3 principal neurons in RSG... These inputs overlap with LR cell bodies and basal dendrites and have been shown to evoke larger excitatory postsynaptic currents in superficial compared to layer 5 pyramidal neurons.
selection_reasoning: This background fact provides context for the study's investigation of DS inputs and their relevance to LR neurons.

fact: Functional responses of RS neurons to claustrum and ACC inputs show significant laminar specificity, with larger EPSPs at lower layer 1 (L1b/c and L1c) and cell body layers compared to upper layer 1 (L1a).
source_span: Population analysis of RS cells revealed significantly larger responses to optogenetic stimulation of ACC inputs at the L1/2 and cell body compared to L1a stimulation... RS cells have the largest EPSP response to ACC inputs at L1/2, while the same minimum LED stimulation power elicits no response in layer 1a.
selection_reasoning: This fact details the laminar specificity of RS neuron responses, supporting the main findings about input targeting.

fact: LR neurons show no significant laminar differences in response to claustrum and ACC inputs, indicating a lack of laminar specificity for these inputs in LR cells.
source_span: LR EPSP amplitudes across all layers were much lower in magnitude and did not differ from responses at L1a... indicating no significant lamination of functional responses to ClaC inputs in the LR population... the much smaller LR EPSP amplitudes across all layers did not differ from responses at L1a.
selection_reasoning: This fact contrasts LR neuron responses with RS neurons, clarifying the specificity of input targeting.

fact: LR dendrites are strongly positively correlated with anterior dorsal thalamic (ADAV) and dorsal subicular (DS) axons, while RS dendrites are strongly correlated with claustrum (CLA) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) axons.
source_span: We found that LR dendrites are strongly and significantly positively correlated with both ADAV and DS axons. In contrast, RS dendrites are strongly correlated with CLA and ACC axons.
selection_reasoning: This anatomical correlation supports the functional findings and reinforces the parallel input pathways to LR and RS neurons.

fact: LR dendrites are significantly negatively correlated with claustrum and anterior cingulate cortex axons, and RS dendrites are negatively correlated with anterior dorsal thalamic and dorsal subicular axons.
source_span: Notably, LR dendrites are significantly negatively correlated with both CLA and ACC axons, and RS dendrites are negatively correlated with ADAV and DS axons.

fact: A two-stage model of heterocyst development in Anabaena involves an initial transient bias in some cells to initiate differentiation followed by competitive resolution mediated by hetR expression and PatS-derived peptides.
source_span: A two-stage model of development in heterocyst-forming cyanobacteria has been proposed [50] . This model posits that during a first stage , only a subset of cells are transiently more likely than others to initiate differentiation prior or at the signal for nitrogen starvation [51] . During the second stage-competitive resolution- the competition between hetR expression and a PatS-derived peptide selects one cell among a cluster of contiguous cells of enhanced hetR expression to differentiate .
selection_reasoning: This model provides a conceptual framework for interpreting the gene expression patterns and differentiation outcomes observed.

fact: Positive correlations in hetR expression between neighboring Anabaena cells support the existence of competitive resolution during heterocyst differentiation.

fact: Prior knowledge about sensory relationships is important for choosing appropriate actions, but this knowledge can be updated through experience.

fact: Learning a simple linear rule relating continuous cues to visuomotor mappings might allow faster generalisation but may not capture complex nonlinearities in the relationship.
